Fix \(k\) and condition on \(\mathcal D_{A,k}\).  By \(\mathrm{ass:empirical-moment-perturbation}\), the learned functions are then fixed, the observations in \(\mathcal C_k\) are conditionally independent, and the stated moment-generating-function bounds hold in every deterministic direction.  Put \(J=J_n\), \(N=n_{C,k}\), and
\[
 M_k=\widehat G_k^C-E[\widehat D_{J_n}^{(-k,A)}\widehat D_{J_n}^{(-k,A)\top}\mid\mathcal D_{A,k}].
\]
Exponential Markov inequality, conditional independence, and the assumed bound for \(X_{i,u}\) imply, for every deterministic unit vector \(u\) and every \(x>0\),
\[
 \Pr\!\left(\left.|u^\top M_ku|>x\ \right|\mathcal D_{A,k}\right)
 \le 2\exp\!\left[-c_1N\min\!\left\{\frac{x^2}{B_{D,n}^4},
 \frac{x}{B_{D,n}^2}\right\}\right].                                      \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, for \(0<\lambda\le c/B_{D,n}^2\), conditional independence gives
\[
 E\!\left[\left.\exp\!\left\{\lambda\sum_{i\in\mathcal C_k}X_{i,u}\right\}\right|\mathcal D_{A,k}\right]
 \le \exp(CN\lambda^2B_{D,n}^4),
\]
and minimizing the exponential-Markov upper bound over the permitted \(\lambda\), then repeating the argument for \(-X_{i,u}\), proves (1).

Let \(\mathcal N_J\) be a \(1/4\)-net of the Euclidean unit sphere with \(|\mathcal N_J|\le9^J\).  The volume comparison proving this bound uses disjoint balls of radius \(1/8\), centered at a maximal \(1/4\)-separated set, all contained in a ball of radius \(9/8\).  For every symmetric matrix \(M\), approximation of a maximizing unit vector by \(\mathcal N_J\) and the triangle inequality give
\[
 \|M\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\max_{u\in\mathcal N_J}|u^\top Mu|.                 \tag{2}
\]
Set \(q_J=J\log(1+J)\).  Substitution of
\[
 x=C_1B_{D,n}^2\left\{\sqrt{q_J/N}+q_J/N\right\}
\]
in (1), followed by (2) and a union bound over \(\mathcal N_J\), makes the conditional exceptional probability arbitrarily small when \(C_1\) is sufficiently large.  Thus, by the definition in \(\mathrm{def:inference-gauges}\),
\[
 \|M_k\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_p\!\left(B_{D,n}^2
 \left\{\sqrt{\frac{J_n\log(1+J_n)}{n_{C,k}}}
 +\frac{J_n\log(1+J_n)}{n_{C,k}}\right\}\right)=O_p(\eta_{G,n}).             \tag{3}
\]

For the cross-moment, define the conditionally centered vector
\[
 V_i=\widehat D_{J_n}^{(-k,A)}(O_i)\widehat B^{(-k,A)}(O_i)
 -E[\widehat D_{J_n}^{(-k,A)}\widehat B^{(-k,A)}\mid\mathcal D_{A,k}],
\]
so that \(u^\top V_i=Z_{i,u}\).  Finiteness of the conditional moment-generating function near zero and its quadratic bound in \(\mathrm{ass:empirical-moment-perturbation}\) imply, by taking the second derivative at zero,
\[
 E[(u^\top V_i)^2\mid\mathcal D_{A,k}]\le C_2B_{D,n}^2B_{0,n}^2.             \tag{4}
\]
Using the coordinate vectors in (4), conditional independence, and conditional centering yields
\[
 E\!\left[\left.\left\|N^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal C_k}V_i\right\|_2^2
 \right|\mathcal D_{A,k}\right]
 =N^{-2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal C_k}\sum_{c=1}^{J}
 E[V_{i,c}^2\mid\mathcal D_{A,k}]
 \le \frac{C_2JB_{D,n}^2B_{0,n}^2}{N}.                                      \tag{5}
\]
Conditional Markov inequality applied to (5) proves an \(O_p(B_{D,n}B_{0,n}\sqrt{J/N})\) bound.  Since \(\log(1+J)\ge\log2\), this is \(O_p(\eta_{c,n})\) under \(\mathrm{def:inference-gauges}\).  Equations (3) and (5) are precisely the two asserted conditional calibration bounds.  Finally, \(K_{\mathrm{fold}}\) is fixed, so a finite union bound makes both conclusions uniform over \(k\); no independence between different folds is needed.

Fix a fold \(k\) and suppress its superscripts.  For a learned bridge cell write
\[
 \Delta h_{aj}=\widehat h_{aj}^{(-k,A)}-h^0_{aj},\qquad
 \Delta q_{a\ell}=\widehat q_{a\ell}^{(-k,A)}-q^0_{a\ell}.
\]
Expanding the definition of \(S_a\) gives the exact identity
\[
 S_a(\widehat h_{aj},\widehat q_{a\ell})-S_a(h^0_{aj},q^0_{a\ell})
 =(1-I_aq^0_{a\ell})\Delta h_{aj}
 +I_a(Y-h^0_{aj})\Delta q_{a\ell}-I_a\Delta q_{a\ell}\Delta h_{aj}.          \tag{6}
\]
Hölder's inequality, \(\mathrm{ass:outcome-learning-rates}\), \(\mathrm{ass:treatment-learning-rates}\), and \(\mathrm{ass:moment-envelope-growth}\) therefore imply, uniformly over retained cells and folds,
\[
 \|S_a(\widehat h_{aj},\widehat q_{a\ell})-S_a(h^0_{aj},q^0_{a\ell})\|_2
 \le M_{q,n}\|\Delta h_{aj}\|_4+M_{y,n}\|\Delta q_{a\ell}\|_4
 +\|\Delta h_{aj}\|_4\|\Delta q_{a\ell}\|_4
 =O_p(d^S_{a,j\ell,n}).                                                       \tag{7}
\]
Each coordinate of the pure and four-corner dictionary is a signed sum of at most four cell signals.  The triangle inequality and the definition of \(d_{c,n}\) in \(\mathrm{def:inference-gauges}\) give
\[
 \|\widehat D-D^0\|_{L^2(P;\ell^2)}^2
 =\sum_{c=1}^{J_n}\|\widehat D_c-D_c^0\|_2^2
 =O_p\!\left(\sum_{c=1}^{J_n}d_{c,n}^2\right).
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \max_k\|\widehat D_{J_n}^{(-k,A)}-D^0_{J_n}\|_{L^2(P;\ell^2)}
 =O_p(\delta_{D,n}),\qquad
 \delta_{D,n}\le\sqrt{J_n}\max_{c\le J_n}d_{c,n}.                           \tag{8}
\]
The same calculation for the two base cells gives
\[
 \max_k\|\widehat B^{(-k,A)}-B^0\|_2=O_p(d_{0,n}),\qquad
 B^0=\sum_{a=0}^1t_aS_a(h^0_{a0},q^0_{a0})=\theta(P)+\phi_0.                  \tag{9}
\]

Put
\[
 G=E[D^0D^{0\top}],\quad c=E[D^0B^0],\quad
 \widetilde G=E[\widehat D\widehat D^\top\mid\mathcal D_{A,k}],\quad
 \widetilde c=E[\widehat D\widehat B\mid\mathcal D_{A,k}].
\]
The population envelope in \(\mathrm{ass:moment-envelope-growth}\) gives
\(\|D^0\|_{L^2(P;\ell^2)}\le\sqrt{J_n}B_{D,n}\) and \(\|B^0\|_2\le B_{0,n}\).  Hence Hilbert-space Cauchy--Schwarz, (8), and (9) yield
\[
 \|\widetilde G-G\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le\|\widehat D-D^0\|_{L^2(\ell^2)}
 \{\|\widehat D\|_{L^2(\ell^2)}+\|D^0\|_{L^2(\ell^2)}\}
 =O_p(2\sqrt{J_n}B_{D,n}\delta_{D,n}+\delta_{D,n}^2),                         \tag{10}
\]
and
\[
 \|\widetilde c-c\|_2
 =O_p\!\left(B_{0,n}\delta_{D,n}
 +(\sqrt{J_n}B_{D,n}+\delta_{D,n})d_{0,n}\right).                            \tag{11}
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem:conditional-calibration-concentration}\), the calibration deviations from \(\widetilde G\) and \(\widetilde c\) are \(O_p(\eta_{G,n})\) and \(O_p(\eta_{c,n})\), respectively.  Equations (10)--(11) and \(\mathrm{def:inference-gauges}\) thus give
\[
 \max_k\|\widehat G_k^C-G\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_p(\zeta_{G,n}),\qquad
 \max_k\|\widehat c_k^C-c\|_2=O_p(\zeta_{c,n}).                             \tag{12}
\]

Let \(\Pi_R=\Pi_{R,J_n}\) denote the orthogonal projection onto \(\operatorname{range}(G)\).  By \(\mathrm{ass:gram-conditioning}\), every positive eigenvalue of \(G\) is at least \(\kappa_{J_n}\), \(0<\tau_n<\kappa_{J_n}/2\), and \(\zeta_{G,n}=o_p(\tau_n)\).  On the event \(\|\widehat G_k^C-G\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\tau_n\), the elementary variational bound
\[
 |u^\top(\widehat G_k^C-G)u|\le\|\widehat G_k^C-G\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\]
shows that empirical eigenvalues corresponding to the population null space are below \(\tau_n\), while the \(\operatorname{rank}(G)\) remaining eigenvalues exceed \(\kappa_{J_n}-o_p(\tau_n)>\kappa_{J_n}/2>\tau_n\).  Thus the thresholded operator
\[
 \widehat G_{k,\tau}=\widehat\Pi_k^C\widehat G_k^C\widehat\Pi_k^C
\]
has the same rank as \(G\), reduced minimum modulus at least \(\kappa_{J_n}/2\), and \(\|\widehat G_{k,\tau}-G\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_p(\zeta_{G,n})\).  Applying the established \(\mathrm{lem:operator-kernel-perturbation}\) to these finite-dimensional self-adjoint operators, and taking complements of their kernel projections, proves
\[
 \max_k\|\widehat\Pi_k^C-\Pi_R\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 =O_p(\zeta_{G,n}/\kappa_{J_n})=O_p(\eta_{\Pi,n}).                            \tag{13}
\]

The population least-squares normal equation is
\[
 Gb_{J_n}=c,\qquad b_{J_n}\in\operatorname{range}(G).                         \tag{14}
\]
To justify \(c\in\operatorname{range}(G)\), if \(v\in\ker G\), then
\(E[(v^\top D^0)^2]=v^\top Gv=0\), so \(v^\top D^0=0\) almost surely and \(v^\top c=E[v^\top D^0B^0]=0\).  By \(\mathrm{def:affine-ensemble-estimator}\), the cutoff-ridge coefficient satisfies
\[
 (\widehat G_k^C+\rho_nI)\widehat b=\widehat\Pi_k^C\widehat c_k^C,\qquad
 \widehat b=\widehat\Pi_k^C\widehat b.                                      \tag{15}
\]
Subtracting (14) from (15), using \(G(I-\Pi_R)=0\), and projecting onto \(\operatorname{range}(G)\) gives the exact equation
\[
 G\Pi_R(\widehat b-b_{J_n})
 =\Pi_R\{(G-\widehat G_k^C)\widehat b+(\widehat c_k^C-c)
 -\rho_n\widehat b-(I-\widehat\Pi_k^C)\widehat c_k^C\}.                    \tag{16}
\]
Because \(c=\Pi_Rc\), (12)--(13) imply
\[
 \|(I-\widehat\Pi_k^C)\widehat c_k^C\|_2
 \le\|\widehat c_k^C-c\|_2+\|(\Pi_R-\widehat\Pi_k^C)c\|_2
 =O_p\{\zeta_{c,n}+\eta_{\Pi,n}\|c\|_2\}.                                 \tag{17}
\]
For every unit \(u\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\(|u^\top c|\le(E[(u^\top D^0)^2])^{1/2}\|B^0\|_2\), and hence
\[
 \|c\|_2\le\sqrt{\Lambda_{J_n}}B_{0,n}.                                   \tag{18}
\]
Invert \(G\) only on its positive eigenspace.  Equations (12), (16)--(18), the lower eigenvalue bound in \(\mathrm{ass:gram-conditioning}\), and the coefficient bound in \(\mathrm{ass:affine-weight-envelope}\) yield
\[
 \max_k\|\Pi_R(\widehat b-b_{J_n})\|_2
 =O_p\!\left[\frac{1}{\kappa_{J_n}}
 \left\{\zeta_{c,n}+(\zeta_{G,n}+\rho_n)L_n
 +\sqrt{\Lambda_{J_n}}B_{0,n}\eta_{\Pi,n}\right\}\right].                 \tag{19}
\]
This retains both the learned-coefficient multiplier on the Gram perturbation and the ridge bias; \(\mathrm{ass:ridge-bias-rate}\) and \(\mathrm{ass:projection-rate}\) make the resulting terms vanish at the declared scale.

Since \(\|v^\top D^0\|_2=\|G^{1/2}v\|_2\le\sqrt{\Lambda_{J_n}}\|\Pi_Rv\|_2\) and
\(\|\widehat b^\top(\widehat D-D^0)\|_2\le L_n\delta_{D,n}\), (8) and (19) prove
\[
 \max_k\|\widehat b^\top\widehat D-b_{J_n}^\top D^0\|_2
 =O_p\!\left[L_n\delta_{D,n}
 +\frac{\sqrt{\Lambda_{J_n}}}{\kappa_{J_n}}
 \left\{\zeta_{c,n}+(\zeta_{G,n}+\rho_n)L_n
 +\sqrt{\Lambda_{J_n}}B_{0,n}\eta_{\Pi,n}\right\}\right].                 \tag{20}
\]

It remains to identify the adjusted signal.  Collecting the coefficient of each cell in the deterministic map of \(\mathrm{def:affine-ensemble-estimator}\) gives, separately for each arm,
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{J_n^h}\sum_{\ell=0}^{J_n^q}\widehat\lambda_{a,j\ell}=1,
 \qquad
 \sum_{a=0}^1t_a\sum_{j,\ell}\widehat\lambda_{a,j\ell}\widehat S_{a,j\ell}
 =\widehat B-\widehat b^\top\widehat D.                                      \tag{21}
\]
The same algebra holds for the population coefficient and weights.  By the established \(\mathrm{lem:normal-affine-identity}\), every coordinate of \(D^0\) lies in \(\mathcal C_P\).  Therefore, for every \(b\), orthogonality of \(\Pi_{\mathcal C_P}\) gives
\[
 \|\phi_0-b^\top D^0\|_2^2
 =\|\phi_0-\Pi_{\mathcal C_P}\phi_0\|_2^2
 +\|\Pi_{\mathcal C_P}\phi_0-b^\top D^0\|_2^2.                             \tag{22}
\]
The normal equation (14) shows that \(b_{J_n}\) minimizes both sides' \(b\)-dependent term, so the last norm in (22) equals \(\alpha_{J_n}\).  Under the hypotheses of the established \(\mathrm{thm:quotient-efficiency}\),
\(\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}=\phi_0-\Pi_{\mathcal C_P}\phi_0\); hence
\[
 \|B^0-b_{J_n}^\top D^0-\theta(P)-\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}\|_2=\alpha_{J_n}.       \tag{23}
\]
Combining (9), (20), (21), and (23) gives exactly
\[
 \max_k\|\widehat\psi^{(-k,C\mid A)}-\theta(P)-\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}\|_2
 =O_p(\Gamma_n).
\]
Finally, \(\mathrm{ass:population-dictionary-approximation}\), \(\mathrm{ass:gram-conditioning}\), and the collected balance \(\mathrm{ass:projection-rate}\) state that this gauge is \(o_p(1)\), proving the last assertion.

For the pointwise result, write \(P_{n,k}\) for the empirical measure on \(\mathcal I_k\) and define the random function
\[
 f_k=\widehat\psi^{(-k,C\mid A)}-\theta(P)-\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}.
\]
The proved \(\mathrm{lem:learned-projection-convergence}\), using all of its displayed nested-split hypotheses, gives
\[
 \max_{k\le K_{\mathrm{fold}}}\|f_k\|_{L^2(P)}=o_p(1).                       \tag{24}
\]
By \(\mathrm{ass:training-measurability}\), \(f_k\) is measurable with respect to
\(\mathcal D_{A,k}\vee\mathcal D_{C,k}\), and the observations in \(\mathcal I_k\) are independent of that sigma-field.  By \(\mathrm{ass:heldout-signal-integrability}\), its conditional second moment is finite with probability tending to one.  Because the fold sizes are proportional to \(n\) and \(K_{\mathrm{fold}}\) is fixed, conditional variance calculation gives
\[
 E\!\left[\left.\left\{\frac{|\mathcal I_k|}{\sqrt n}(P_{n,k}-P)f_k\right\}^2
 \right|\mathcal D_{A,k}\vee\mathcal D_{C,k}\right]
 \le C\|f_k\|_2^2=o_p(1).                                                     \tag{25}
\]
Conditional Chebyshev inequality and a finite union bound therefore show
\[
 \sum_{k=1}^{K_{\mathrm{fold}}}\frac{|\mathcal I_k|}{\sqrt n}(P_{n,k}-P)f_k=o_p(1). \tag{26}
\]

We next control the conditional drift without assuming that learned signal convergence already includes it.  For one learned cell, the exact expansion (6), outcome-bridge solvability, and treatment-bridge solvability imply
\[
 P\{S_a(\widehat h,\widehat q)-S_a(h^0,q^0)\}
 =-E[I_a(\widehat q-q^0)(\widehat h-h^0)].                                    \tag{27}
\]
Indeed, the expectation of the first term in (6) is
\(E[(\widehat h-h^0)\{1-T_a^*q^0\}]=0\), and that of the second is
\(E[I_a(\widehat q-q^0)\{g_a-T_ah^0\}]=0\).  Conditioning the last term in (27) first on \((A,Z,X)\) and then on \((W,X)\), and applying Cauchy--Schwarz in the respective Hilbert spaces, yields both bounds
\[
 |E[I_a\Delta q\Delta h]|
 \le\|T_a\Delta h\|_{\mathcal G_a}\|\Delta q\|_{\mathcal G_a},
 \qquad
 |E[I_a\Delta q\Delta h]|
 \le\|\Delta h\|_{\mathcal H}\|T_a^*\Delta q\|_{\mathcal H}.             \tag{28}
\]
The weights in (21) sum to one within each arm, and their total variation is at most \(L_n\) by \(\mathrm{ass:affine-weight-envelope}\).  Thus (27)--(28), \(\mathrm{ass:outcome-residual-rate}\), \(\mathrm{ass:adjoint-residual-rate}\), and the \(L^2\) parts of \(\mathrm{ass:outcome-learning-rates}\) and \(\mathrm{ass:treatment-learning-rates}\) give
\[
 \max_k|P\widehat\psi^{(-k,C\mid A)}-\theta(P)|
 =O_p\!\left(L_n\min\{r_{h,n}e_{q,2,n},r_{q,n}e_{h,2,n}\}\right)
 =o_p(n^{-1/2}),                                                               \tag{29}
\]
where the last equality is \(\mathrm{ass:primitive-mixed-bias-rate}\).

Since the folds partition the sample, equations (26)--(29) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sqrt n\{\widehat\theta_n-\theta(P)\}
 &=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}(O_i)
 +\sum_k\frac{|\mathcal I_k|}{\sqrt n}(P_{n,k}-P)f_k
 +\sum_k\frac{|\mathcal I_k|}{\sqrt n}Pf_k\\
 &=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}(O_i)+o_p(1).              \tag{30}
 \end{aligned}
\]
By \(\mathrm{thm:quotient-efficiency}\), \(E[\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}]=0\) and
\(E[\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}^2]=V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\).  The theorem assumes this variance is in \((0,\infty)\).  For every \(\epsilon>0\), dominated convergence gives
\[
 E[\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}^2\mathbf1\{|\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}|>\epsilon\sqrt n\}]\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus the frozen \(\mathrm{lem:lindeberg-feller-central-limit}\), applied to
\(X_{ni}=n^{-1/2}\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}(O_i)\) using \(\mathrm{ass:iid-sampling}\), and then Slutsky's theorem applied to (30), prove
\[
 \sqrt n\{\widehat\theta_n-\theta(P)\}\Rightarrow N\{0,V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\}. \tag{31}
\]

For variance estimation, (24), conditional Markov inequality, and the same foldwise conditioning give
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf_{k(i)}(O_i)^2=o_p(1).                                   \tag{32}
\]
Empirical Cauchy--Schwarz makes the cross term between \(f_{k(i)}(O_i)\) and
\(\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}(O_i)\) negligible.  It remains only to use a law of large numbers for \(\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}^2\) under a finite first moment.  For \(M<\infty\), the average of
\(\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}^2\wedge M\) converges by Chebyshev's inequality, while Markov's inequality bounds the empirical tail probability by a constant times
\(E[\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}^2\mathbf1\{\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}^2>M\}]\), which tends to zero as \(M\to\infty\).  Therefore
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}(O_i)^2\to_pV_{\mathrm{eff}}(P).       \tag{33}
\]
Equations (30), (32), and (33) imply
\[
 \widehat V_n
 =\frac1n\sum_i\{\widehat\psi_i-\theta(P)\}^2
 -\{\widehat\theta_n-\theta(P)\}^2
 \to_pV_{\mathrm{eff}}(P).
\]
Positivity of \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\) gives ratio consistency.  Slutsky's theorem and continuity of the standard normal distribution at
\(\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\) then prove the asserted pointwise Wald coverage.

We finally prove the locally uniform extension without invoking the unresolved score-lifting question.  Let
\[
 \Xi_n=\{(s,t):s\in\mathcal S,\ |t|\le T\},\qquad
 Q_{n,\xi}=P_{n,t,s}\quad(\xi=(s,t)),
\]
and abbreviate
\(\theta_{n,\xi}=\theta(Q_{n,\xi})\),
\(\phi_{n,\xi}=\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}(Q_{n,\xi})\), and
\(V_{n,\xi}=E_{Q_{n,\xi}}[\phi_{n,\xi}^2]\).
The locally uniform hypotheses explicitly require the hypotheses of
\(\mathrm{thm:quotient-efficiency}\), including tangent equality and pathwise product validity, at every \(Q_{n,\xi}\).  Thus that theorem identifies \(\phi_{n,\xi}\) as the canonical gradient at each such law; this is an assumed local-law premise, not a resolution of \(\mathrm{oeq:score-lifting-completeness}\).

Take an arbitrary deterministic sequence \(\xi_n=(s_n,t_n)\in\Xi_n\) and put \(Q_n=Q_{n,\xi_n}\).  Rerunning (6)--(23) under \(Q_n\) is legitimate because every approximation, bridge-learning, multiplier, calibration-concentration, eigenvalue-gap, cutoff, coefficient, weight, and projection-gauge hypothesis used there is assumed uniformly over \(\Xi_n\).  It yields
\[
 \max_k\|\widehat\psi_{n,k}-\theta(Q_n)-\phi_{n,\xi_n}\|_{L^2(Q_n)}=o_{Q_n}(1). \tag{34}
\]
The uniform root-\(n\) mixed-bias condition similarly makes (29) \(o_{Q_n}(n^{-1/2})\).  Conditional evaluation-fold Chebyshev applied under \(Q_n\) then repeats (25)--(30), so
\[
 \sqrt n\{\widehat\theta_n-\theta(Q_n)\}
 =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_{n,\xi_n}(O_i)+o_{Q_n}(1).                 \tag{35}
\]
Because the sequence \(\xi_n\) was arbitrary, (35) is uniform.  More explicitly, if its remainder were not uniformly \(o_p(1)\), there would be \(\delta>0\), \(\epsilon>0\), a subsequence, and choices \(\xi_n\) on that subsequence for which its probability exceeded \(\delta\), contradicting the sequencewise conclusion just proved.  This is the contradiction form of the subsequence principle, and it also applies below.

To compare the changing gradients in one Hilbert space, let
\[
 \mathsf J_{n,\xi}f=f\sqrt{dQ_{n,\xi}/dP}:L^2(Q_{n,\xi})\longrightarrow L^2(P).
\]
It is an isometry, since
\(\|\mathsf J_{n,\xi}f\|_{L^2(P)}^2=E_{Q_{n,\xi}}[f^2]\).  The assumed uniform transported \(L^2(P)\) convergence therefore gives
\[
 \sup_{\xi\in\Xi_n}|V_{n,\xi}-V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)|\longrightarrow0.           \tag{36}
\]
Moreover, all likelihood ratios in \(\mathcal V_P\) lie between \(1-\varepsilon\) and \(1+\varepsilon\).  Hence, for every fixed \(\epsilon>0\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &E_{Q_{n,\xi}}[\phi_{n,\xi}^2\mathbf1\{|\phi_{n,\xi}|>\epsilon\sqrt n\}]\\
 &\quad\le E_P[(\mathsf J_{n,\xi}\phi_{n,\xi})^2
 \mathbf1\{|\mathsf J_{n,\xi}\phi_{n,\xi}|>\epsilon\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}\sqrt n\}],
 \end{aligned}                                                               \tag{37}
\]
which tends to zero uniformly by the assumed uniform integrability of the transported squared family; this also verifies the separately stated uniform Lindeberg condition.  For every sequence \(\xi_n\), the frozen
\(\mathrm{lem:lindeberg-feller-central-limit}\), (36), and (37) give
\[
 n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_{n,\xi_n}(O_i)\Rightarrow N\{0,V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\}
 \quad\text{under }Q_{n,\xi_n}^n.                                             \tag{38}
\]
The subsequence principle again turns (38) into uniform convergence in distribution over \(\Xi_n\), for example in bounded-Lipschitz distance.  Combining it with (35) proves the asserted uniform centered Gaussian limit.

The variance proof is uniform as well.  Along every sequence \(\xi_n\), conditional Markov inequality applied to (34) gives the analogue of (32).  For the leading squares, truncate \(\phi_{n,\xi_n}^2\) at \(M\).  Chebyshev's inequality controls the bounded triangular-array average by \(M/n\), and uniform integrability in (37) controls both its empirical and population tails uniformly as \(M\to\infty\).  Thus
\[
 \sup_{\xi\in\Xi_n}Q_{n,\xi}^n
 \!\left(\left|\widehat V_n-V_{n,\xi}\right|>\epsilon\right)\longrightarrow0
 \qquad(\epsilon>0).                                                         \tag{39}
\]
Equations (36) and (39), together with \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)>0\), prove uniform ratio consistency and, with (35)--(38), uniform Wald coverage for \(\theta(Q_{n,\xi})\).

Finally, the displayed uniform LAN expansion and mutual contiguity ensure that these \(Q_{n,\xi}^n\) are the declared contiguous local experiments and that base-law and local-law negligible events are interchangeable.  The assumed target expansion gives
\[
 \sqrt n\{\theta(Q_{n,\xi})-\theta(P)\}
 =tE_P[\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)s]+o(1)                                         \tag{40}
\]
uniformly.  Consequently, under \(Q_{n,\xi}^n\), centering at \(\theta(P)\) adds the local shift in (40), while centering at the true local target \(\theta(Q_{n,\xi})\) removes it and leaves the common limit in (38).  This is regularity on the declared uniformly controlled contiguous classes.  Since \(\mathrm{thm:quotient-efficiency}\) makes each \(\phi_{n,\xi}\) canonical and (36) makes its variance converge to \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\), the attained limiting variance is the local semiparametric efficiency bound.

prose_updates.tldr: The observed-law model uses the full local \(L^\infty\) likelihood-ratio ball, the full fixed-defect spectrally separated operator stratum, and every DQM curve that remains in both bridge-solvability loci. Reverse score lifting on this unrestricted joint germ remains unresolved: continuous kernel projections do not themselves parameterize the coupled solvability intersection. Conditional on tangent equality and the theorem's explicit pathwise product condition, the quotient projection is valid.
